name: Prepositional Verb-Particle-Object Construction
pattern: Head:V + Comp:PP[particle, Head:P[intransitive]] + Od:NP ↔ Head:V + Od:NP + Comp:PP[particle, Head:P[intransitive]]

entry.name: Prepositional Verb-Particle-Object Construction
entry.pattern: Head:V + Comp:PP[particle, Head:P[intransitive]] + Od:NP ↔ Head:V + Od:NP + Comp:PP[particle, Head:P[intransitive]]

dimensions.form: VP headed by a verb with an NP direct object and a separate one-word PP complement in particle use, ordered either Head–particle–Od or Head–Od–particle
dimensions.meaning: Ranges from transparent spatial or directional combinations to aspectual and idiomatic verb-particle combinations
dimensions.function: Allows a one-word PP complement to occur exceptionally between the verb head and its NP direct object
dimensions.distribution: VP-internal in transitive clauses; post-object order is required with an unstressed personal-pronoun Od, while lexical and information-weight factors affect the two orders elsewhere

1.definition: A one-word PP complement in particle use combines with a verb and a distinct NP direct object
1.details: Particle is a syntactic use, not a lexical category. In the central case, the particle is a one-word PP headed by an intransitive preposition. In She took off the label, off is a complement of take and the label is a separate Od; this differs from She jumped off the wall, where off is a transitive preposition and off the wall is a single PP complement. The particle construction is diagnosed by order alternation, obligatory pre-particle placement of an unstressed pronoun, and the failure of particle + Od to behave as a constituent (CGEL Ch. 4 §6.2, pp. 280–83).

examples.note: Head–particle–Od order with down as a one-word PP complement
Post-object particle; compare the impossible unstressed-pronoun order *took off it

constraints.description: The particle is a Comp:PP of the verb and the NP is a separate Od of the verb; particle + NP is not a PP constituent.
In the central prepositional subtype recorded here, the particle is a one-word PP headed by an intransitive P; the term particle identifies its syntactic use rather than a lexical category.
An ordinary non-pronominal Od generally permits Head–particle–Od and Head–Od–particle orders, but an unstressed personal-pronoun Od must immediately follow the verb: take it off, not *take off it.
Particle + Od cannot normally be fronted, foregrounded in an it-cleft, or repeated as a coordinated phrase; these failures distinguish the sequence from a transitive PP.
Heavy-NP postposing and lexical fossilisation can obscure the ordinary alternation, so no single placement test is necessary in every token.

projection.target: The ability of a one-word PP complement to intervene between Head:V and a non-pronominal Od predicts a corresponding post-object placement, obligatory pre-particle placement of an unstressed pronoun, and non-constituency of particle + Od
projection.evidence: CGEL's order, pronoun-substitution, fronting, coordination, and adverb-insertion contrasts jointly distinguish the particle construction from V + transitive-PP structure (Ch. 4 §6.2, pp. 280–83).

core.property: One-word PP complement in particle use

diagnostics: unstressed personal pronoun immediately follows V

core.property: Particle plus Od is not a constituent

activation_states.effect: End placement of the Od may be licensed independently of the particle construction
One of the two particle positions may be strongly preferred or excluded

known_boundary_items: jump off the wall: off heads a transitive PP containing its own Obj, rather than a particle PP followed by Od
read through the prospectus versus read the prospectus through: CGEL treats this as alternation between a transitive PP and NP plus non-particle intransitive PP
Adjectival and verbal particles occur in a small set of idioms, but the present entry records the central PP subtype

relatedConstructions.notes: The particle and direct object are dependents in a VP headed by V
The separate direct object is realized by an NP
The particle is a one-word PP complement

grounds.note: Particle is a syntactic use; central particles are one-word PPs headed by intransitive prepositions

curious.title: Little words before or after an object
curious.summary: A short word like down or off can come before or after the object of a verb, as in brought down the bed and brought the bed down.
curious.body: In She brought down the bed, the small word down goes with the verb brought, and the bed is what she brought. The same thing can be said the other way: She brought the bed down. In the dictionary's account, down isn't the start of a phrase down the bed. It stands on its own beside the verb, and the bed is a separate object. The dictionary marks this account as provisional, and says no single test works in every case.
curious.try: Say took the label off, then try replacing the label with it. Where does it go?

teacher.summary: Helps explain verb-particle combinations with an object, including word-order flexibility and the pronoun restriction.
teacher.explain: In this construction a verb takes a separate noun phrase as direct object and a one-word prepositional phrase complement in particle use. The particle is a syntactic use, not a word category. In She took off the label, off is a complement of take and the label is a separate direct object. This differs from She jumped off the wall, where off heads a prepositional phrase containing its own object. An ordinary object generally allows both orders, but an unstressed personal-pronoun object must immediately follow the verb: take it off. This dictionary marks its analysis provisional, and notes that heavy objects and fixed idioms can obscure the alternation.
teacher.terms: Sometimes called a verb-particle combination or a phrasal verb; the second label also covers cases without an object. In this grammar the particle is a one-word prepositional phrase complement of the verb.

contrasts.note: An unstressed pronoun object cannot follow the particle; this dictionary gives take it off.

watch_for: A learner might read down the bed in brought down the bed as a single phrase, when this dictionary treats down and the bed as separate.
A learner might treat take off it like take off the label, though an unstressed pronoun must come before the particle.
teacher.activity: Give students phrasal verbs on cards (take off, bring down, put on). They build sentences with a noun object in both orders, then replace the object with it and say where the particle must go.

child.hook: Can you say "took the label off" and "took off the label"?
child.explain: Some small words like off and down can go before or after the object. She took the label off. She took off the label. With it, the little word goes after it.
child.play: Take a sticker off a page and say what you did two ways. Then say what you did with it, like "I took it off."

checked.note: Fixed: child explanation no longer says the particle goes on either side of 'what the verb moves' (many combinations involve no movement); now says before or after the object; curious title reworded likewise; 'the entry' replaced by 'this dictionary'; phrasal verb hedged as a broader label. Second round: fixed child.explain, comes last changed to goes after it (the entry requires the particle to follow an unstressed pronoun object, not to end the sentence); cut the curious claim that separateness is why both orders are possible; teacher.explain now says an ordinary object generally allows both orders, as the entry does.
